message.content:
A **custodial IRA** is a retirement account opened for a minor by an adult custodian (typically a parent, grandparent, or legal guardian). The account is legally owned by the child, but the adult manages it until the minor reaches the age of majority—usually 18 or 21, depending on state laws. At that point, control transfers to the child and the account becomes a regular IRA.

## Key Features

- **Types**: A custodial IRA can be either a **Traditional IRA** or a **Roth IRA**, though Roth IRAs are more commonly recommended for minors.
- **Earned Income Requirement**: The child must have earned income (W-2 wages or self-employment income like babysitting or lawn mowing) to contribute. The contribution limit is the lesser of the annual IRA limit ($7,000 for 2024-2025) or the child's total earned income.
- **No Age Minimum**: Even very young children can contribute as long as they have reportable earned income.
- **Tax Advantages**: 
  - **Roth**: Contributions are made with after-tax dollars; earnings grow tax-free, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
  - **Traditional**: Contributions may be tax-deductible; earnings grow tax-deferred, but withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income.

## Why Roth Is Often Preferred for Minors

Most children are in low or zero tax brackets, so they gain little benefit from the upfront tax deduction of a Traditional IRA. A Roth IRA allows them to pay minimal or no taxes now and enjoy decades of tax-free growth.

## Flexibility

- Contributions (but not earnings) can be withdrawn at any time without penalty.
- Exceptions allow penalty-free withdrawals of earnings for qualified education expenses or a first-time home purchase (up to $10,000 lifetime).

## Important Notes

- The custodian cannot withdraw funds for personal use.
- Anyone can contribute to the account as a gift, as long as total contributions don't exceed the child's earned income or annual limits.
- Custodial IRAs follow all standard IRS rules for regular IRAs regarding contributions, taxes, and distributions.

Sources:
1. https://www.nerdwallet.com/article/investing/why-your-kid-needs-a-roth-ira
2. https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-is-custodial-ira/

6. https://www.birchgold.com/blog/retirement/gold-custodial-iras/
7. https://verdence.com/insight/custodial-roth-ira/
8. https://nopassiveincome.com/custodial-roth-ira-vs-ugma/
9. https://www.wealthenhancement.com/blog/custodial-roth-ira-build-child-wealth
